solution.concept_anchor: Bhadrabahu and Sthulabhadra — Jain schism
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because Bhadrabahu is indeed a central figure in the Jain schism, but he is associated with the Digambara tradition that migrated south, not with remaining in Magadha.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Bhadrabahu is linked to the Digambara group that departed, not to those who remained and compiled texts in Magadha.
Eliminate option c: The schism is traditionally dated to around 300 BCE during Chandragupta Maurya's reign — not to the Gupta period.

Eliminate option d: The Jain schism's proximate cause was a famine-driven migration and disagreement over monastic practice, not a doctrinal dispute about the nature of the founder — that better describes the Buddhist split.
Confirm option b: Sthulabhadra is associated with those who remained in Magadha and is the figure linked to the Shvetambara tradition.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: A student who has read superficially about the Jain schism knows Bhadrabahu is the key figure but may not recall whether it was Bhadrabahu or Sthulabhadra who remained in Magadha. The trap places Bhadrabahu in the role belonging to Sthulabhadra. Additionally, the Jain and Buddhist schisms are commonly conflated — the Buddhist schism centred on doctrinal differences about the Buddha's nature, while the Jain schism centred on monastic practice and canonical authority during a famine.
solution.final_explanation:
The Jain schism is traditionally dated to around 300 BCE, during a severe famine in Magadha coinciding with the reign of Chandragupta Maurya. The monk Bhadrabahu, sensing the famine's severity, led a group of followers southward to Karnataka, where strict monastic observance including nudity could be maintained. Those who remained in Magadha were led by Sthulabhadra and adopted white robes as a concession to conditions — this group became the Shvetambara tradition. The group that migrated became the Digambara tradition.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Bhadrabahu led the migrating group southward; he is the Digambara patriarch, not the leader of those remaining in Magadha.
• Option (b): Correct. Sthulabhadra led those remaining in Magadha, and his followers developed into the Shvetambara tradition.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The schism is dated to approximately 300 BCE, not to the Gupta period (4th–6th century CE).
• Option (d): Incorrect. The Jain schism was not primarily about the nature of the founder — that characterises the Theravada-Mahayana Buddhist split.

Value Addition:
• The Buddhist schism (Theravada vs. Mahayana) centred on the Bodhisattva ideal and the nature of the Buddha — structurally different from the Jain schism.
• Chandragupta Maurya's alleged conversion to Jainism and his death by Sallekhana at Shravanabelagola is a Digambara claim.
• The First Jain Council at Pataliputra was convened in Bhadrabahu's absence — its authority is rejected by Digambaras on that basis.

solution.concept_anchor: Digambara–Shvetambara core doctrinal differences

statement_analysis.statement: The Digambara sect holds that complete nudity is a prerequisite for liberation because any possession, including clothing, constitutes parigraha.
statement_analysis.reason: Digambaras interpret aparigraha (non-possession) to its logical extreme — even clothing is a form of attachment and must be renounced for moksha.

statement_analysis.statement: The Shvetambara sect teaches that women cannot attain moksha in their current birth and must be reborn as men before achieving liberation.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the Digambara position, not the Shvetambara position. Shvetambaras explicitly hold that women can attain moksha and cite Malli (19th Tirthankara) as a female example.

statement_analysis.statement: Both Digambara and Shvetambara traditions accept a canon of 24 Tirthankaras but disagree on the gender of the 19th Tirthankara, Malli.
statement_analysis.reason: Shvetambaras identify Malli as female; Digambaras insist Malli was male — this is a direct textual disagreement between the two sects.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is a strong distractor because all three statements appear plausible on first reading, and a student who conflates the female-moksha position with Shvetambara rather than Digambara will accept Statement 2 as correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Digambara doctrine holds any possession including clothing is parigraha — Statement 1 is correct.
Check Statement 2: The position that women cannot attain moksha in their current birth belongs to Digambaras, not Shvetambaras — Statement 2 is incorrect, eliminating options a and d.
Verify Statement 3: Both sects accept 24 Tirthankaras but disagree on Malli's gender — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 1 and 3 are correct — the answer is option c (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The most dangerous trap here is Statement 2, which assigns the denial of female moksha to Shvetambaras. A student who has memorised the two sects' names without internalising which position belongs to which will easily mistake this. The Digambara position denies female moksha and identifies Malli as male; the Shvetambara position affirms female moksha and identifies Malli as female. This reversal is a classic UPSC-style entity-swap distractor.
solution.final_explanation:
The Digambara–Shvetambara divide rests on several interlocking doctrinal positions. Understanding which belief belongs to which sect is more important than knowing the beliefs in isolation.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Digambara doctrine treats nudity as mandatory for liberation because even clothing represents attachment (parigraha). Aparigraha, the fifth Mahavrata, is taken to its logical extreme in Digambara monastic practice.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The belief that women cannot attain moksha in their current birth is the Digambara position, not the Shvetambara position. Shvetambaras hold that women can attain liberation and point to Malli (19th Tirthankara) as evidence.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Both sects agree on the 24-Tirthankara framework but diverge sharply on whether Malli was male (Digambara) or female (Shvetambara) — a direct canonical disagreement.

Value Addition:
• 'Digambara' literally means 'sky-clad' (dik = sky/directions, ambara = clothed); 'Shvetambara' means 'white-clad' (shveta = white, ambara = clothed).
• The disagreement over Malli's gender is one of the sharpest textual disputes in Jain sectarian literature.
• Shvetambara nuns hold full monastic status; Digambara nuns are considered spiritually inferior to monks in the traditional hierarchy.

solution.concept_anchor: Jain councils and Agama canonical dispute

statement_analysis.statement: The Second Jain Council was held at Valabhi and resulted in the final compilation of the Shvetambara canon under the scholar Devardhigani.
statement_analysis.reason: The Second Jain Council at Valabhi (approximately 5th century CE) was presided over by Devardhigani and produced the authoritative Shvetambara scriptural canon — this statement is factually accurate.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Jain Council at Pataliputra was convened to compile Buddhist canonical texts after Ashoka's patronage, and is therefore claimed by both Jain and Buddhist traditions.
statement_analysis.reason: The First Jain Council at Pataliputra (~300 BCE) was convened in Bhadrabahu's absence to compile Jain scriptures — it has no connection to Buddhist canonical compilation or Ashoka's patronage. Buddhist councils were separate events held at Rajagriha, Vaishali, and Pataliputra.

statement_analysis.statement: The Digambara sect participated in the Valabhi Council but subsequently rejected its authority on doctrinal grounds.
statement_analysis.reason: Digambaras did not participate in the Valabhi Council — their non-participation is the very basis for rejecting its authority. The claim that they participated but later repudiated it is factually wrong.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is the only fully correct statement; a student who identifies it as correct might assume it is one of the 'incorrect' ones being asked about and second-guess themselves.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: The Valabhi Council under Devardhigani compiled the Shvetambara canon — this is accurate, so Statement 1 is NOT incorrect.
Check Statement 2: The First Jain Council at Pataliputra was a Jain event, not a Buddhist one — conflating it with Buddhist councils makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Check Statement 3: Digambaras did not participate in Valabhi; non-participation is the basis for rejection, not post-participation repudiation — Statement 3 is also incorrect.
Both Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect — the answer is option b (2 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The city of Pataliputra hosted both a Jain council and a Buddhist council, creating a notorious confusion trap. A student who has memorised 'Pataliputra council' without distinguishing between the Jain and Buddhist versions will mix up the events. Statement 2 deliberately introduces Ashoka and Buddhist texts to exploit this conflation. Statement 3 exploits the subtler error of assuming Digambaras attended Valabhi — in fact, their absence is the root of their rejection of the resulting canon.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain councils are among the most examination-relevant topics precisely because they share city names with Buddhist councils, enabling cross-tradition confusion traps.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Second Jain Council at Valabhi (approximately 453 or 512 CE) under Devardhigani compiled the final Shvetambara canon. This statement is factually accurate and does NOT belong in the 'incorrect' category.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The First Jain Council at Pataliputra (~300 BCE) was an exclusively Jain event to compile scriptures in Bhadrabahu's absence. Ashoka's Buddhist patronage and Buddhist canonical compilation were entirely separate events. This statement incorrectly conflates the two traditions.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Digambaras never participated in the Valabhi Council. Their non-participation is precisely why they reject its authority. Saying they attended but later repudiated it reverses the actual sequence.

Value Addition:
• Buddhist councils: First at Rajagriha, Second at Vaishali, Third at Pataliputra (Ashoka's reign), Fourth in Kashmir (Kanishka's reign).
• The 12th Anga, Drishtivaada, is considered lost by both Jain sects.
• Digambaras hold that Mahavira's original teachings are entirely irrecoverable — a radical position distinguishing them from Shvetambaras.

solution.concept_anchor: Jain sub-sects and their defining practices

statement_analysis.statement: Bisapantha (Digambara) — allows idol worship with flowers and material offerings
statement_analysis.reason: Bisapantha is the more liberal Digambara sub-sect that permits elaborate idol worship including flowers, lamps, and offerings, and is dominant in South India.

statement_analysis.statement: Terapanthi (Shvetambara) — founded by Bhikshu in the 18th century; governed by a single centralised Acharya
statement_analysis.reason: The Shvetambara Terapanthi movement was indeed founded by Acharya Bhikshu in the 18th century and is distinguished by its highly centralised monastic structure under one supreme Acharya.

statement_analysis.statement: Taranpantha (Digambara) — rejects idol worship entirely; founded in the 15th century by Taran Svami
statement_analysis.reason: Taranpantha, founded by Taran Svami in the 15th century, completely rejects idol worship and represents the closest approximation to a reform movement within Digambara tradition.

statement_analysis.statement: Sthanakvasi (Shvetambara) — the oldest Shvetambara sub-sect; accepts temple worship and is the most traditional branch
statement_analysis.reason: Sthanakvasi emerged around the 17th century and rejects idol worship and temples; it is the Murtipujaka sub-sect that is the oldest and most traditional idol-worshipping Shvetambara branch.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) is a strong distractor because three pairs are indeed correct; a student who incorrectly accepts the Sthanakvasi description without checking its defining feature of rejecting temples will mark all four as correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Bisapantha: It is the liberal Digambara sub-sect permitting flowers and offerings — the pairing is correct.
Verify Shvetambara Terapanthi: Founded by Bhikshu, 18th century, single Acharya — correct.
Verify Taranpantha: Founded by Taran Svami, 15th century, rejects idols — correct.

Check Sthanakvasi: It rejects idol worship and emerged around the 17th century — it is NOT the oldest or most traditional Shvetambara sub-sect; that is Murtipujaka. This pairing is incorrect — only three pairs are correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Sthanakvasi pairing is the trap. A student who remembers only that Sthanakvasi is a Shvetambara sub-sect may accept the description without recalling that it actually rejects temples and emerged relatively late (17th century). The description given — 'oldest,' 'most traditional,' 'accepts temple worship' — accurately describes Murtipujaka, not Sthanakvasi. This entity-swap within the same tradition is a sophisticated distractor.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain sub-sects form a layered structure beneath the two major traditions. Knowing the defining practice of each sub-sect is essential, as UPSC questions frequently swap attributes between sub-sects of the same parent tradition.

| Jain Sub-sect | Parent Tradition | Key Feature |
|---|---|---|
| Bisapantha | Digambara | Liberal; permits flower/lamp offerings in idol worship |
| Terapanthi | Digambara | Stricter; minimalist worship, no flowers or lamps |
| Taranpantha | Digambara | Rejects idol worship entirely; founded 15th century |
| Murtipujaka | Shvetambara | Oldest; traditional idol-worshipping sub-sect |
| Sthanakvasi | Shvetambara | Rejects idols and temples; emerged ~17th century |
| Terapanthi | Shvetambara | Founded by Bhikshu, 18th century; single Acharya |

• Pair 4 (Sthanakvasi) is incorrect — the correct description of Sthanakvasi is a temple-rejecting, non-idol-worshipping sub-sect, not the 'oldest and most traditional.'

Value Addition:
• 'Terapantha' exists in BOTH traditions — Digambara Terapantha (minimalist worship) and Shvetambara Terapantha (Bhikshu's reform movement) are unrelated despite sharing a name.
• Sthanakvasi monks carry a muhapatti (mouth-covering cloth) as a symbol of non-harm to airborne organisms.
• Taranpantha is sometimes considered closer to a nirguna devotional movement than a mainstream Jain sect.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because it correctly places the Gomateshwara statue with Shravanabelagola and Digambara but misattributes the Dilwara Temples' patron (swapping Vimal Shah with a Digambara patron), exploiting the fact that many students know Dilwara is Jain but not specifically Shvetambara.
elimination_logic: Identify A (Dilwara Temples): Built by Vimal Shah under Solanki/Chaulukya rulers in Rajasthan — Shvetambara tradition, matching with 3.
Identify B (Gomateshwara statue): 57-foot monolith at Shravanabelagola built under Ganga minister Chavundaraya — Digambara, matching with 1.
Identify C (Mahamastakabhisheka): Head-anointing ceremony held every 12 years at Shravanabelagola — Digambara identity marker, matching with 4.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The primary trap lies in attributing the Dilwara Temples. Students know Dilwara is a Jain temple complex but may not know it belongs specifically to the Shvetambara tradition, built under the Solanki/Chaulukya dynasty by Vimal Shah and Tejpal. Swapping Digambara attribution to Dilwara (option a) is designed to catch students who know the temple exists but have not fixed its sectarian identity. Similarly, Mahamastakabhisheka is a culturally prominent ritual but is specifically Digambara — associating it with Shvetambara rites is another potential confusion.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain monumental architecture is divided along sectarian lines, and UPSC questions routinely test whether students can correctly assign a monument to its sect and patron.

• A (Dilwara Temples) — Shvetambara (3): Built at Mount Abu, Rajasthan, by Vimal Shah and Tejpal under the Solanki (Chaulukya) rulers. Famous for intricate white marble carving. Firmly Shvetambara.
• B (Gomateshwara / Bahubali statue) — Digambara (1): The 57-foot monolithic statue at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka, commissioned by Ganga dynasty minister Chavundaraya. The nude, unadorned statue reflects Digambara iconographic norms.
• C (Mahamastakabhisheka) — Digambara (4): The head-anointing ceremony performed every 12 years at Shravanabelagola. One of the largest religious gatherings in India; exclusively Digambara in tradition.
• D (Ranakpur Temple) — Shvetambara (2): Located in Rajasthan, built under the patronage of the Solanki period merchant Dhanna Shah; architecturally elaborate and firmly Shvetambara.

Correct match: A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2.

Value Addition:
• Digambara icons are unadorned, eyes cast downward, no garments — reflecting total detachment.
• Shvetambara icons have inlaid glass eyes, are dressed and ornamented — reflecting a different conception of the liberated soul.
• The Dilwara Temples (Vimal Vasahi and Luna Vasahi) are considered among the finest examples of marble craftsmanship in medieval India.

solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is a classic 'both true but unconnected' assertion-reason design. A student who reads A (Shvetambara icons have open eyes and ornaments) and R (Shvetambaras identify Malli as female) will instinctively sense both are true Shvetambara positions and select option a. However, the iconographic style of open eyes derives from the Shvetambara belief about the embodied nature of the omniscient Kevali — not from any position about Malli's gender. These are two independent doctrinal elements that happen to coexist within Shvetambara theology.
solution.final_explanation:
Shvetambara and Digambara traditions diverge sharply on both iconography and the gender of specific Tirthankaras, but these two positions are theologically independent of each other.

Assertion A: Correct. Shvetambara Tirthankara images are characterised by open eyes (inlaid glass), ornamental dress, and garments. This iconographic convention reflects the Shvetambara belief that the Kevali (omniscient being) continues to interact with and perceive the world, retaining sensory consciousness even after attaining omniscience.

Reason R: Correct. Shvetambaras identify Malli, the 19th Tirthankara, as female. Digambaras counter that Malli was male. This is one of the sharpest direct textual disagreements between the two sects.

• Digambara icons are nude, eyes cast downward, unadorned — reflecting total withdrawal from the world after omniscience.
• The Shvetambara belief that the Kevali still eats and sleeps is directly opposed by Digambaras, who hold the Kevali transcends all bodily functions.
• Malli's gender remains one of the most cited examples of direct canonical disagreement between the two sects.

solution.concept_anchor: Chronology of Jain and Buddhist councils
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because it correctly places the First Jain Council before the Second Jain Council but reverses the Buddhist councils, exploiting uncertainty about whether the Third Buddhist Council (Pataliputra) came before or after Vaishali.
elimination_logic: The First Jain Council at Pataliputra is dated to ~300 BCE — this is the earliest event among the four.
The Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra occurred during Ashoka's reign (~250 BCE) — after the First Jain Council but before the Valabhi Council.
The Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir is associated with Kanishka's reign (~1st–2nd century CE) — later than the Third Buddhist Council.

The Second Jain Council at Valabhi is dated to ~453–512 CE — the latest of all four events. Correct order: First Jain Council → Third Buddhist Council → Fourth Buddhist Council → Second Jain Council = option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits two common confusions: first, that the city Pataliputra hosted both a Jain council and a Buddhist council (different events requiring different dates), and second, uncertainty about the relative ordering of the Third Buddhist Council (Ashoka, ~250 BCE) and the Fourth (Kanishka, ~1st–2nd century CE). A student who knows these councils in isolation but has not fixed their timeline relative to each other will struggle to sequence them correctly.
solution.final_explanation:
Placing Jain and Buddhist councils on a common timeline requires distinguishing events that share city names from those that do not.

Correct sequence:
1. First Jain Council, Pataliputra (~300 BCE) — convened in Bhadrabahu's absence during the famine; produced texts rejected by Digambaras.
2. Third Buddhist Council, Pataliputra (~250 BCE) — held during Ashoka's reign to purify the Sangha; associated with Moggaliputta Tissa.
3. Fourth Buddhist Council, Kashmir (~1st–2nd century CE) — held under Kanishka's patronage; associated with the Sarvastivada school and Mahayana developments.
4. Second Jain Council, Valabhi (~453–512 CE) — compiled the final Shvetambara Agamic canon under Devardhigani.

Wrong options fail because they misplace the Valabhi Council before the Buddhist councils or reorder the Buddhist councils internally.

Value Addition:
• First Buddhist Council: Rajagriha, immediately after the Buddha's death (~483 BCE); Second Buddhist Council: Vaishali (~383 BCE).
• The Second Jain Council at Valabhi is the Shvetambara canon's definitive moment — Digambaras reject its output entirely.
• Pataliputra (modern Patna) hosted major councils of two different religions in different centuries — a classic cross-tradition confusion point.

solution.concept_anchor: Sallekhana — Jain philosophical basis vs. legal characterisation
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because students aware of the 2015 Rajasthan High Court ruling may recall it was declared illegal, and may not know the Supreme Court subsequently stayed that ruling, making b's framing of the HC ruling as having final effect misleading.
elimination_logic: The scenario describes a gradual, voluntary, conscious fast at the end of natural life — this matches the Jain concept of Sallekhana (also called Santhara), not passive euthanasia or suicide under any conventional definition.

Eliminate option b: The Rajasthan HC ruled Sallekhana illegal in 2015, but the Supreme Court stayed that ruling — the HC decision does not have final legal effect; this option overstates the HC's authority.

Eliminate option c: Sallekhana is considered by Jain philosophy to be a conscious, non-violent death undertaken without passion — the opposite of suicide, which in Jain thought involves an act driven by passion or despair.

Eliminate option d: Aparigraha refers to non-possession/non-attachment; while related to Jain ethics, it is not the primary doctrinal basis for Sallekhana — the correct principle is ahimsa applied to the self, combined with a conscious, gradual exit from life. Option a correctly identifies Sallekhana and its contested legal status under Article 21.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option b exploits the student's knowledge that the Rajasthan High Court did declare Sallekhana illegal in 2015 — this is accurate but incomplete. The Supreme Court issued a stay on that ruling, preserving the practice's legal ambiguity. A student who recalls only the HC ruling without knowing about the Supreme Court stay will select b. Additionally, option c's characterisation of Sallekhana as suicide is the exact framing the Jain community contests — the philosophical distinction (no passion, gradual, voluntary) is what makes option c a well-constructed wrong answer.
solution.final_explanation:
Sallekhana (also known as Santhara) is the Jain practice of voluntarily and gradually reducing food and water intake at the end of life, undertaken with full awareness and without the emotional passion that Jain philosophy associates with negative karma. It is practiced by both Digambara and Shvetambara traditions, though more visibly associated with Digambaras.

The scenario describes the classic conditions under which Sallekhana is permitted: terminal or extreme old age, voluntary decision, gradual process, and conscious intent.

• Option (a): Correct. The practice is Sallekhana. The 2015 Rajasthan High Court ruling declared it illegal as a form of suicide, but the Supreme Court stayed that order — the legal status remains contested, with the Jain community invoking religious freedom under Articles 25 and 26 against the right-to-life framework of Article 21.
• Option (b): Incorrect. While the HC ruling is factually referenced, it does not have final legal force because of the Supreme Court's stay — this option creates a false sense of finality.
• Option (c): Incorrect. In Jain philosophy, Sallekhana is explicitly distinguished from suicide: suicide involves passion or despair; Sallekhana is detached, conscious, and non-violent.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Aparigraha (non-attachment) is a broader Jain ethical principle; while philosophically connected, it is not the direct doctrinal basis invoked for Sallekhana.

Value Addition:
• The Digambara tradition holds that Chandragupta Maurya himself died by Sallekhana at Shravanabelagola after abdicating and following Bhadrabahu south.
• Sallekhana's legal battle involves Article 25 (freedom of religion), Article 26 (management of religious affairs), and Article 21 (right to life — interpreted to include right not to be forced to live).
• The Supreme Court stay means the Rajasthan HC order has no operative effect pending final adjudication.

solution.concept_anchor: Jain epistemological doctrines — Anekantavada, Syadvada, Nayavada
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Saptabhangi) is a strong distractor because it is a highly technical Jain term that many students may not immediately recognise as a component of Syadvada, and may instead confuse it with a Buddhist logical concept.
elimination_logic: Anekantavada — doctrine of many-sidedness of truth; core Jain epistemological contribution — belongs to the Jain philosophical system.
Nayavada — doctrine of partial standpoints; explicitly stated to be a component of Anekantavada — belongs to the Jain system.
Saptabhangi — the seven-fold predication scheme within Syadvada — belongs to the Jain system.
Pratityasamutpada — the Buddhist doctrine of dependent origination; it has no connection to Jain philosophy and is the odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Saptabhangi is placed as a potential odd one out to test whether students recognise it as a Jain term. A student who has not encountered Saptabhangi may confuse it with a Buddhist concept and select it as the odd one out. Pratityasamutpada, while a well-known Buddhist concept, is presented alongside three genuine Jain terms — the correct identification requires knowing all four terms, not just the most familiar ones.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain philosophy made significant epistemological contributions, and three of the four options here are from that same doctrinal family.

• Option (a) Anekantavada: Jain doctrine of the many-sidedness of reality — no single perspective captures the whole truth. Core Jain philosophical contribution.
• Option (b) Pratityasamutpada: Buddhist doctrine of dependent origination — the principle that all phenomena arise in dependence upon conditions. This is a Buddhist concept and does NOT belong to the Jain epistemological system. This is the odd one out.
• Option (c) Saptabhangi: The seven-fold predication scheme within Syadvada; each proposition about reality is qualified by 'syat' (in some sense). A component of the Jain logical system.
• Option (d) Nayavada: Doctrine of partial standpoints — each viewpoint captures one aspect of reality. Explicitly described as a component of Anekantavada within Jain philosophy.

Value Addition:
• Syadvada and Anekantavada are often confused with the Buddhist Middle Path — they are structurally different; Jain conditional logic is a distinct epistemological claim, not a moral/practical path.
• Pratityasamutpada underpins Buddhist metaphysics — no permanent self or substance, all phenomena are causally conditioned.
• Anekantavada is sometimes invoked in modern discourse as a philosophical basis for pluralism and tolerance.

solution.concept_anchor: Sectarian disagreements on Mahavira's life and Kevala Jnana

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 1: The Digambara tradition holds that Mahavira was a lifelong celibate who never married, while the Shvetambara tradition accepts that he was married to Yashoda and had a daughter.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a direct and well-documented sectarian disagreement: Digambaras maintain Mahavira's lifelong celibacy; Shvetambaras accept his marriage to Yashoda and fatherhood.

statement_analysis.statement: Statement 2: Both the Digambara and Shvetambara sects agree that after attaining Kevala Jnana, the omniscient Tirthankara continues to perform normal bodily functions including eating and sleeping.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the Shvetambara position only. Digambaras hold that after Kevala Jnana, the Tirthankara completely transcends bodily functions — no eating, sleeping, or physical processes continue.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because Statement 1 is unambiguously correct, and students who read Statement 2 quickly may interpret 'continues to perform normal bodily functions' as a neutral fact about humanity rather than recognising it as a sect-specific (Shvetambara-only) doctrinal position.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Digambara tradition = lifelong celibate Mahavira; Shvetambara = married to Yashoda. This distinction is well-established — Statement 1 is correct.

Test Statement 2: The qualifier 'Both sects agree' is the trap. Only Shvetambaras hold the Kevali continues bodily functions; Digambaras hold the Kevali transcends all bodily processes after omniscience.
Statement 2 is incorrect — eliminate options a and b.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — the answer is option c.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 is the word 'Both.' A student who knows the Shvetambara position on the embodied Kevali may not register that this is a sect-specific, not universally shared, belief. The Digambara counter-position — that the Kevali completely transcends bodily functions — is a nuanced doctrinal point that distinguishes these traditions at a philosophical (not just ritual) level. Students who have studied only one sect's position on Kevala Jnana are most vulnerable to accepting Statement 2 as a general Jain belief.
solution.final_explanation:
These two statements test whether students can correctly assign doctrinal positions to their respective sects without confusing shared beliefs with sect-specific ones.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Digambara–Shvetambara divide on Mahavira's personal life is one of the sharpest biographical disagreements in Jain sectarian literature. Digambaras insist on Mahavira's complete celibacy from birth; Shvetambaras accept the narrative of his marriage to Yashoda and the birth of a daughter. The embryo-transfer story (from a Brahmin woman to a Kshatriya womb) is also a Shvetambara-specific narrative rejected by Digambaras.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The statement falsely attributes to both sects a position that belongs only to Shvetambaras. Shvetambaras hold that even after attaining Kevala Jnana (omniscience), the Tirthankara continues to eat, sleep, and engage in normal bodily functions. Digambaras directly reject this — in their view, omniscience marks the complete transcendence of physical existence.

Value Addition:
• Both sects agree that Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana under a sal tree and attained nirvana at Pavapuri — these are shared biographical elements.
• The embryo-transfer story in Shvetambara texts says Mahavira's embryo was transferred from a Brahmin womb to the Kshatriya womb of Trishala — this is rejected entirely by Digambaras.
• The Digambara view of the Kevali (transcending all bodily functions) is theologically consistent with their view that the omniscient being is fully liberated even before physical death.

solution.concept_anchor: Etymology of Digambara and Shvetambara sect names
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because 'white-robed' and 'unadorned' are both associated with Jain monastic practice, and a student who knows Digambara means 'sky-clad' may misconstrue the Sanskrit components and select c.
elimination_logic: Recall that 'Digambara' derives from 'dik' (directions/sky) + 'ambara' (clothed) — meaning 'sky-clad' or clothed by the directions, i.e., naked.
Recall that 'Shvetambara' derives from 'shveta' (white) + 'ambara' (clothed) — meaning 'white-clad.'
The blank requires both etymologies in correct order — 'sky-clad' for Digambara and 'white-clad' for Shvetambara.
Option a provides the correct pairing — Digambara = sky-clad, Shvetambara = white-clad.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option c reverses the etymological meanings — assigning 'white-clad' to Digambara and 'sky-clad' to Shvetambara. A student who has memorised the terms by association (Digambara = stricter = nudity) but has not fixed the literal Sanskrit etymology may confuse which word means what when presented with reversed options. The trap is purely linguistic — both terms are familiar, but their Sanskrit derivations can be confused under exam pressure.
solution.final_explanation:
The names of the two major Jain sects are etymologically descriptive of their most distinctive monastic practice.

• Option (a): Correct. 'Digambara' derives from Sanskrit 'dik' (sky, directions) + 'ambara' (clothing), meaning 'sky-clad' — i.e., wearing the sky itself, which means nudity. 'Shvetambara' derives from 'shveta' (white) + 'ambara' (clothing), meaning 'white-clad.' This pairing is accurate.
• Option (b): Incorrect. 'Forest-dweller' and 'renunciant' are not the etymological meanings of either term.
• Option (c): Incorrect. This reverses the meanings — assigning 'white-clad' to Digambara and 'sky-clad' to Shvetambara.
• Option (d): Incorrect. 'Earth-robed' is not the meaning of Digambara; this is a fabricated distractor.

Value Addition:
• Both sect names encode their most visible monastic distinction — dress (or its absence).
• The Shvetambara monk's white cloth is unstitched, reflecting minimal attachment to material form.
• The Digambara practice of nudity is considered the ultimate expression of aparigraha (non-possession) — even the body's covering is a form of attachment.

solution.concept_anchor: Jain sectarian geography and royal patronage
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because Chandragupta Maurya and Jainism are genuinely connected, but the specific claim that it is a Shvetambara tradition to link his conversion narrative is incorrect — this is exclusively a Digambara tradition.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Shvetambara stronghold is northern India (Rajasthan, Gujarat) — not Karnataka; Karnataka is Digambara territory.
Eliminate option b: The narrative of Chandragupta Maurya converting to Jainism and dying by Sallekhana at Shravanabelagola is a Digambara claim, not a Shvetambara one.
Eliminate option c: The Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu belong to the Shvetambara tradition, patronised by the Solanki dynasty — not the Ganga dynasty.

Confirm option d: The Ganga dynasty (Karnataka) were patrons of the Digambara tradition, and the Gomateshwara statue was commissioned under the Ganga minister Chavundaraya — this pairing is correctly matched.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a exploits geographic confusion — students who know Shvetambara is a major Jain sect may not have fixed the north-south sectarian geography, and may accept Karnataka as a plausible Shvetambara location. Option b is a subtler trap: Chandragupta Maurya and Jainism are genuinely connected, but the connection is specifically a Digambara claim — assigning it to Shvetambara is a precise entity-swap.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain sectarian geography follows a clear north-south divide that is regularly tested.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Shvetambara's stronghold is northern India — Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Punjab — not Karnataka. Karnataka is the Digambara heartland.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The tradition of Chandragupta Maurya converting to Jainism, abdicating, and dying by Sallekhana at Shravanabelagola is a Digambara narrative, not Shvetambara.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu, Rajasthan, were built under Solanki (Chaulukya) patronage — specifically by Vimal Shah and Tejpal. They are Shvetambara monuments, not Ganga dynasty.
• Option (d): Correct. The Ganga dynasty of Karnataka were major Digambara patrons. The Gomateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola was commissioned by Chavundaraya, the minister of the Ganga king — a definitive Digambara monument in Digambara territory.

Value Addition:
• Shvetambara patronage: Chalukyas of Gujarat (Solanki), Oswal and Porwal merchant communities of Rajasthan.
• Digambara patronage: Gangas, Hoysalas, Rashtrakutas of Karnataka.
• Ranakpur Temple (Rajasthan) — also Shvetambara, built under mercantile patronage during the 15th century.

solution.concept_anchor: Jain karma as physical substance; Mahavrata vs. Parshvanatha

statement_analysis.statement: In Jain philosophy, karma is conceived as a physical substance that attaches to the soul (jiva), distinguishing it from both Hindu and Buddhist conceptions of karma as a moral or mental force.
statement_analysis.reason: Jain karma theory explicitly describes karma as a fine material substance (pudgala) that adheres to the soul — this is a uniquely Jain metaphysical claim, not shared by Hindu or Buddhist karma theories.

statement_analysis.statement: Parshvanatha, the 23rd Tirthankara, prescribed five great vows (Mahavratas) for his followers, to which Mahavira added a sixth — brahmacharya — creating the complete monastic code.
statement_analysis.reason: Parshvanatha prescribed four vows (chaturyama — ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha). Mahavira's contribution was adding brahmacharya as the fifth vow, making five Mahavratas total — not six. There is no sixth vow.

statement_analysis.statement: Digambara tradition emphasises extreme austerities, including nudity, as a primary means of shedding accumulated karma (nirjara), while Shvetambara allows a more moderate path to the same end.
statement_analysis.reason: Nirjara (shedding of karma) is the mechanism for liberation in Jain philosophy; Digambaras hold extreme austerity including nudity is essential, while Shvetambaras accept a more moderate monastic path.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d (all three correct) is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are correct, and Statement 2 sounds authoritative — a student who knows Parshvanatha had fewer vows but misremembers the count (thinking four became six) may accept Statement 2.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: Jain karma as a physical substance (pudgala) is a foundational Jain metaphysical claim distinguishing it from Hindu and Buddhist karma — Statement 1 is correct.

Check Statement 2: Parshvanatha had four vows (chaturyama); Mahavira added brahmacharya as the fifth, making five Mahavratas — not a sixth vow. Statement 2 falsely says Mahavira added a 'sixth.' Statement 2 is incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Digambara emphasis on extreme austerity (nudity) as a tool for nirjara vs. Shvetambara's moderate path — correctly characterises the sectarian divide. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — the answer is option a (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is carefully constructed to be almost right: the factual kernel (Parshvanatha had fewer vows, Mahavira added one) is correct, but the statement says Mahavira added brahmacharya as a 'sixth' vow, implying Parshvanatha already had five. In reality, Parshvanatha had four (chaturyama), and Mahavira's addition of brahmacharya brought the total to five — not six. This is a classic partial-truth trap where the distractor gets the relationship right but gets the number wrong.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain ethics and metaphysics contain several precisely defined technical elements whose numbers and attributions are frequently tested.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Jain karma theory is philosophically distinctive. Unlike the Hindu concept of karma as moral causation or the Buddhist concept as mental volition, Jainism describes karma as a fine physical substance (a category of pudgala/matter) that literally adheres to the soul based on thought, word, and deed. This is examinable both in Prelims (direct fact) and Mains (comparative philosophy).
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Parshvanatha's monastic code comprised four vows — chaturyama (ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha). Mahavira's reform added brahmacharya (celibacy) as the fifth vow, completing the five Mahavratas. There is no sixth vow — the statement's claim that Mahavira added a 'sixth' is arithmetically and doctrinally wrong.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Nirjara (the active shedding of accumulated karma through austerity) is central to both sects, but Digambaras take it to its extreme conclusion — complete nudity, minimal possessions, severe fasting — while Shvetambaras accept a less extreme monastic path as sufficient.

Value Addition:
• Eight types of karma (Ashtakarma): Jnanavaraniya (knowledge-obscuring), Darshanavaraniya (perception-obscuring), Mohaniya (deluding), Antaraya (obstructive) — plus Vedaniya, Ayushya, Nama, Gotra.
• Samvara (stopping new karma) and Nirjara (shedding old karma) together lead to moksha in Jain philosophy.
• Both sects observe the same five Mahavratas for monks and five Anuvratas (lesser vows) for lay followers.

solution.concept_anchor: Digambara nuns — spiritual status in monastic hierarchy
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because it partially reflects Digambara belief (nuns cannot achieve moksha) but incorrectly states they are barred from the monastic order entirely — Digambara nuns do exist and observe 28 mula-gunas; they simply occupy an inferior position in the spiritual hierarchy.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: Digambara tradition does not bar women from the monastic order — nuns exist and observe 28 mula-gunas; the limitation is on their capacity to achieve moksha, not their membership in the sangha.
Eliminate option c: Shvetambara nuns have full monastic status equal to monks — the 'equal but separate' framing with inferior doctrinal status applies to Digambara nuns, not Shvetambara.
Eliminate option d: The fourfold sangha (monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen) is a shared framework of both sects — it is not unique to Shvetambara.

Confirm option b: In Digambara tradition, nuns observe 28 mula-gunas and have a recognised monastic status, but are considered spiritually inferior to monks in the hierarchy and cannot achieve liberation without first being reborn as men.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option a is the most dangerous distractor: it correctly captures the Digambara belief that women cannot attain moksha but incorrectly extends this to a complete bar on joining the monastic order. This is a scope-extension error — the restriction is on moksha-attainment, not on sangha membership. Students who conflate 'cannot achieve liberation' with 'cannot be nuns' will select option a.
solution.final_explanation:
The status of nuns is one of the sharpest practical expressions of the Digambara–Shvetambara theological divide on female liberation.

• Option (a): Incorrect. Digambara tradition does not prohibit women from entering the monastic order. Digambara nuns exist and are required to follow 28 mula-gunas (foundational rules of conduct). The limitation is specifically on their capacity to attain moksha in their current female birth — not on monastic membership itself.
• Option (b): Correct. Digambara nuns follow 28 mula-gunas and hold a recognised position within the sangha, but in Digambara theological hierarchy they are considered spiritually inferior to monks and incapable of achieving final liberation without first being reborn in a male body.
• Option (c): Incorrect. This describes Digambara nuns, not Shvetambara. Shvetambara nuns hold full monastic status equal to monks, with no doctrinal inferiority assigned.
• Option (d): Incorrect. The fourfold sangha (monks/nuns/laymen/laywomen) is a structural feature common to both major Jain sects, not unique to Shvetambara.

Value Addition:
• Shvetambaras cite Malli (19th Tirthankara, identified as female) as definitive proof that women can attain moksha — directly counter to Digambara position.
• The 28 mula-gunas for Digambara nuns include rules on food, movement, possessions, and interaction with laypeople.
• Both sects have laywomen (shravika) who observe the five Anuvratas — the lay ethical code applicable to both genders.

statement_analysis.statement: Jainism's survival in India, in contrast to Buddhism's near-disappearance, is primarily attributed to royal patronage secured by Jain monks at the courts of the Maurya and Gupta empires.
statement_analysis.reason: Jainism's survival is attributed to its deep integration with merchant and trading communities, not dependence on royal patronage. statement_analysis.statement: The Dilwara Temples at Mount Abu and the Ranakpur Temple in Rajasthan were both constructed under mercantile patronage associated with the Shvetambara tradition.
statement_analysis.reason: Both Dilwara (Vimal Shah, Tejpal under Solanki rulers) and Ranakpur (Dhanna Shah under Rana Kumbha's patronage) were financed by Shvetambara-associated merchants — this is historically accurate.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because a student might identify Statement 2 as incorrect and then second-guess whether Statement 3 is also incorrect (confusing Ranakpur's patronage), potentially selecting b (Statements 2 and 3) instead of c (Statement 2 only).
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Oswal, Porwal, Shrimali communities of Rajasthan and Gujarat are indeed the Shvetambara lay constituency — Statement 1 is correct, not a candidate for the 'incorrect' answer.
Check Statement 2: Jainism's survival is attributed to merchant-community integration, not royal patronage; the reversal is historically wrong — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Check Statement 3: Both Dilwara and Ranakpur were built under Shvetambara-associated mercantile patronage — Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statement 2 is incorrect — the answer is option c (2 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a common confusion between the reasons for Jainism's survival and Buddhism's decline. Students who know both religions had royal patronage at various times may not have fixed the key analytical distinction: Jainism integrated deeply into merchant communities and became financially self-sustaining at the lay level, while Buddhism became heavily dependent on institutional monastic support funded by royal/elite patronage — a vulnerability exposed when that patronage withdrew or when Islamic invasions disrupted monastic centres.
solution.final_explanation:
The social and economic basis of Jainism's survival is a comparative history question that connects geography, patronage, and community structure.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Oswal, Porwal, and Shrimali communities of Rajasthan and Gujarat form the core Shvetambara lay constituency and are among India's most prominent trading communities. Their deep identification with Shvetambara Jainism has funded temple construction, sustained monastic orders, and preserved the tradition through political disruptions.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement inverts the correct historical analysis. Jainism's resilience in India is attributed precisely to its integration with merchant and lay trading communities — not royal patronage. Buddhism's relative decline in India is partly explained by its greater dependence on institutional (monastic) and royal patronage, which became vulnerable when Islamic incursions destroyed monastic centres and royal support shifted.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Both the Dilwara Temples (built by Vimal Shah and Tejpal under Solanki/Chaulukya patronage) and the Ranakpur Temple are products of Shvetambara mercantile patronage in Rajasthan.

Value Addition:
• Digambara trading communities in Karnataka and Maharashtra (Komiati, Chettiar connections) similarly sustained that tradition through lay patronage.
• The destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila monasteries by Bakhtiyar Khilji (~1200 CE) is considered a major blow to institutional Buddhism in India.
• Jainism never centralised its learning in a few large monasteries — dispersed lay community integration made it more resilient.

solution.concept_anchor: Jain vs. Buddhist schism — causes, timelines, doctrinal depth

statement_analysis.statement: The Jain schism between Digambara and Shvetambara was primarily triggered by a disagreement over monastic practice (dress code) and canonical authority, rather than a fundamental divide over the nature of the founder.
statement_analysis.reason: Unlike the Buddhist Theravada–Mahayana split, which involved deep doctrinal disagreements about the Buddha's nature and the Bodhisattva ideal, the Jain schism was primarily about monastic practice (nudity vs. white robes) and acceptance of canonical texts.

statement_analysis.statement: The Theravada–Mahayana split in Buddhism involved a deeper doctrinal divide, including disagreements over the Bodhisattva ideal and the nature of the Buddha, compared to the Jain sectarian split.
statement_analysis.reason: The Buddhist schism is characterised by profound philosophical and soteriological disagreements — the Mahayana Bodhisattva ideal, the nature of Buddha as transcendent, and the path to liberation — distinguishing it structurally from the Jain schism.

statement_analysis.statement: Both the Jain schism and the Theravada–Mahayana Buddhist split are dated to the same century — the 3rd century BCE — and were triggered by the same political event: Ashoka's patronage of Buddhism.
statement_analysis.reason: The Theravada–Mahayana split is conventionally placed in the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE period, well after the Jain schism (~300 BCE). More importantly, the Jain schism was not triggered by Ashoka's patronage — it was precipitated by a famine and Bhadrabahu's southward migration.

statement_analysis.statement: The First Jain Council at Pataliputra and the Third Buddhist Council also at Pataliputra were different events from different religious traditions held in the same city, though both are associated with the post-Mauryan period.
statement_analysis.reason: The Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra is directly associated with Ashoka's reign (~250 BCE) — firmly within the Mauryan period, not post-Mauryan. The First Jain Council (~300 BCE) was held during Chandragupta Maurya's reign — also Mauryan period. 'Post-Mauryan' is incorrect for both.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c (Only three) is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 2 are clearly correct; students who correctly reject Statement 3 but fail to scrutinise the 'post-Mauryan' claim in Statement 4 will mark three as correct.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Jain schism was over monastic practice and canonical authority, not the nature of the founder — correct.
Statement 2: Theravada–Mahayana split involved deeper doctrinal divides (Bodhisattva, Buddha's nature) — correct.
Statement 3: The Theravada–Mahayana split is NOT dated to the 3rd century BCE and was NOT triggered by Ashoka's patronage of Buddhism — this conflates different events and periods. Incorrect.

Statement 4: The Third Buddhist Council was during Ashoka's reign (Mauryan period), and the First Jain Council was also during Chandragupta Maurya's reign — both are Mauryan period events, not post-Mauryan. Incorrect. Only two statements are correct — answer is option b (Only two).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 4 contains a subtle temporal error: calling both councils 'post-Mauryan' when both occurred during the Mauryan period. A student focused on identifying the more obvious error in Statement 3 (the same-century/Ashoka claim) may not pause to verify Statement 4's 'post-Mauryan' qualifier. This two-layer trap is designed for students who correctly eliminate Statement 3 but accept Statement 4 uncritically, leading them to select 'Only three' instead of 'Only two.'
solution.final_explanation:
Comparing the Jain and Buddhist schisms requires precision about both doctrinal content and chronology.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Digambara–Shvetambara split centred on monastic dress and canonical legitimacy — not the founder's nature. This is structurally different from the Buddhist schism.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Theravada–Mahayana divide is philosophically deeper — involving the Bodhisattva ideal (delayed personal liberation for the sake of all beings), a transcendent conception of the Buddha, and different understandings of the liberation path.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Two errors. First, the Theravada–Mahayana split is not dated to the 3rd century BCE — it developed over the 1st century BCE to 1st century CE. Second, the Jain schism was not triggered by Ashoka's patronage — it was precipitated by a famine and Bhadrabahu's migration, separate from Ashoka entirely.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Both councils referenced occurred during the Mauryan period — the Third Buddhist Council during Ashoka (~250 BCE) and the First Jain Council during Chandragupta Maurya (~300 BCE). Calling them 'post-Mauryan' is factually wrong.

Value Addition:
• The Fourth Buddhist Council (Kashmir, Kanishka's reign) is the one most associated with Mahayana developments — not Ashoka's Third Council.
• Both the Jain and Buddhist schisms illustrate how institutional crises (famine, doctrinal disputes) lead to lasting sectarian divisions.
• The Jain schism produced two traditions that coexist without major violent conflict — unlike some Buddhist sectarian disputes.

solution.concept_anchor: Chandragupta Maurya — Digambara narrative vs. Ashoka conversion
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because both A and R are correct, and the causal link appears superficially plausible — Chandragupta's migration to Shravanabelagola does validate the Digambara southward migration narrative — but R does not explain A; the Digambara claim about Chandragupta is not the reason the Gomateshwara statue was commissioned centuries later.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion A correct? Shravanabelagola is indeed the site of the monolithic Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue, commissioned under Ganga minister Chavundaraya — yes, A is factually correct.

Step 2 — Is Reason R correct? The Digambara tradition does claim Chandragupta Maurya converted to Jainism, abdicated, followed Bhadrabahu to Karnataka, and died by Sallekhana at Shravanabelagola — yes, R is factually correct as a statement of Digambara tradition.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? No. The Gomateshwara statue depicts Bahubali (son of Rishabhanatha, the 1st Tirthankara) — not Chandragupta Maurya. Chandragupta's presence at Shravanabelagola explains why the site is sacred in Digambara tradition, but it does not explain why the statue of Bahubali/Gomateshwara was commissioned there by Chavundaraya of the Ganga dynasty. The two are historically and iconographically separate.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — the answer is option b.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are genuine Digambara-tradition facts about Shravanabelagola, making the association feel intuitively correct. The trap is that the Gomateshwara statue depicts Bahubali — a figure from Jain cosmological history (son of Rishabhanatha) — not Chandragupta Maurya. Chandragupta's narrative explains Shravanabelagola's sacred importance to Digambaras, but the statue was commissioned separately by Chavundaraya to honour Bahubali. R is a true fact about the site but not the causal explanation for the statue.
solution.final_explanation:
Shravanabelagola holds multiple layers of Digambara significance, and separating them is essential for causal reasoning in assertion-reason questions.

Assertion A: Correct. The 57-foot monolithic Gomateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka, is a defining Digambara monument. It was commissioned by Chavundaraya, a minister of the Ganga dynasty, in the 10th century CE. The statue depicts Bahubali (also called Gomateshwara), the son of the first Tirthankara, Rishabhanatha.

Reason R: Correct as a statement of Digambara tradition. The Digambara account holds that Chandragupta Maurya, after abdicating, converted to Jainism under Bhadrabahu, migrated to Karnataka, and eventually died by Sallekhana at Shravanabelagola — this validates the site's deep Digambara significance.

Causal link: R does not explain A. The Gomateshwara statue depicts Bahubali, not Chandragupta. Chavundaraya's 10th-century commission was an act of devotion to Bahubali, not a commemoration of Chandragupta. While R explains why Shravanabelagola is sacred to Digambaras, it does not explain why or how the Gomateshwara statue was built.

Value Addition:
• Mahamastakabhisheka — the head-anointing ceremony for the Gomateshwara statue — is performed every 12 years and is one of India's largest religious gatherings.
• Bahubali is venerated in both Digambara and Shvetambara traditions as the first human to attain omniscience in the current cosmic cycle.
• Ashoka (not Chandragupta) converted to Buddhism — a common UPSC confusion point between the two Mauryan emperors.

solution.concept_anchor: Terapantha — two distinct sub-sects in different traditions
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is deceptive because it assigns to 'Terapantha' (without specifying the tradition) the characteristics of the Digambara Terapantha, which a student may accept as the 'standard' Terapantha without realising there is a separate Shvetambara Terapantha with different origins and practices.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: This describes Digambara Terapantha (minimalist, no flowers or lamps) — not the Shvetambara Terapantha founded by Bhikshu. Conflating the two is the trap.
Eliminate option b: Taranpantha is the Digambara sub-sect that completely rejects idol worship, founded by Taran Svami in the 15th century — not Terapantha.
Eliminate option d: Murtipujaka is the traditional idol-worshipping Shvetambara sub-sect — distinct from Terapanthi (Shvetambara), which is a reform movement founded in the 18th century.

Confirm option c: Shvetambara Terapanthi was founded by Acharya Bhikshu in the 18th century and is distinguished by its highly centralised structure under a single Acharya — the correct and complete description.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The name 'Terapantha' exists in both Digambara and Shvetambara traditions with entirely different origins, founders, and beliefs. A student who has studied only one of these will apply its characteristics to the other. Option a gives the Digambara Terapantha's characteristics (minimalist worship, no lamps) — a student who has only studied Digambara sub-sects will recognise this description and select it without realising the question specifically asks about Shvetambara Terapanthi. This is one of the most reliable UPSC confusion traps in Jain sub-sect questions.
solution.final_explanation:
The existence of 'Terapantha' as a name in both major Jain traditions is a well-known examination trap.

• Option (a): Incorrect. This describes Digambara Terapantha — the stricter, minimalist Digambara sub-sect that avoids flowers, lamps, and elaborate offerings. It is not the Shvetambara Terapanthi.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Rejecting idol worship entirely and founding in the 15th century describes Taranpantha (Digambara), founded by Taran Svami — a distinct sub-sect.
• Option (c): Correct. The Shvetambara Terapanthi movement was founded by Acharya Bhikshu (also called Swami Bhikhanji) in the 18th century. Its distinguishing feature is a highly centralised monastic organisation under a single supreme Acharya, with a strict interpretation of ahimsa and internal discipline.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Murtipujaka is the oldest Shvetambara sub-sect — the traditional idol-worshipping group. It is not Terapanthi.

Value Addition:
• Digambara Terapantha (minimalist) and Shvetambara Terapanthi (Bhikshu's reform) share only a name — their origins, founders, dates, and practices are entirely different.
• Shvetambara Terapanthi monks carry a muhapatti (mouth cover) and rajoharan (broom) and are strictly governed by the ruling Acharya.
• Sthanakvasi (Shvetambara) also rejects idol worship but is a separate sub-sect from Terapanthi — both emerged from reformist impulses but at different times.

solution.concept_anchor: Shvetambara Agamic canon — 12 Angas and Drishtivaada

statement_analysis.statement: The Shvetambara sect accepts 12 Angas as authentic canonical scriptures, compiled and finalised at the Second Jain Council held at Valabhi.
statement_analysis.reason: The 12 Angas form the core of the Shvetambara Agamic canon, and their final compilation is attributed to the Council of Valabhi under Devardhigani in approximately the 5th century CE.

statement_analysis.statement: The 12th Anga, Drishtivaada, is considered lost by both Digambara and Shvetambara sects, making it the only point of canonical agreement between them.
statement_analysis.reason: While both sects acknowledge the loss of Drishtivaada, calling it 'the only point of canonical agreement' is an overstatement — the two sects share other agreements (24 Tirthankaras, five Mahavratas, etc.). The Digambara position is more radical: they reject all existing Agamas, not just note the loss of Drishtivaada.

statement_analysis.statement: The Digambara position on canonical scriptures is that Mahavira's original teachings are entirely irrecoverable — a more radical stance than simply rejecting the Valabhi compilations.
statement_analysis.reason: Digambaras hold not merely that the Valabhi council was unauthorized, but that the original Jain canon as taught by Mahavira has been entirely lost and cannot be reconstructed — a fundamentally more radical textual position.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option d is a strong distractor because students who identify Statements 1 and 3 as correct might be uncertain about Statement 2 and default to selecting all three as correct.
elimination_logic: Verify Statement 1: 12 Angas compiled at Valabhi Council — this is the standard Shvetambara canonical account. Statement 1 is correct.

Check Statement 2: 'The only point of canonical agreement' is an overstatement — Digambara and Shvetambara share many foundational agreements (Tirthankaras, Mahavratas). The claim of 'only' makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Verify Statement 3: Digambara position that Mahavira's teachings are entirely irrecoverable is a more radical claim than simply rejecting Valabhi — Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — the answer is option a (1 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses the qualifier 'only point of canonical agreement' to convert a true partial claim (both sects acknowledge Drishtivaada is lost) into a false absolute. A student who knows both sects accept the loss of Drishtivaada will identify the factual kernel as true and miss the overstatement introduced by 'only.' This scope-extension mechanism is one of the most reliable UPSC distractor techniques.
solution.final_explanation:
The Agamic canon dispute is a foundational source of Digambara–Shvetambara tension and is frequently tested in both Prelims and Mains.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Shvetambara canonical tradition recognises 12 Angas as the authoritative scriptural corpus. The Second Jain Council at Valabhi (approximately 453 or 512 CE), presided over by Devardhigani, is credited with their final compilation. This council and its output are rejected by Digambaras.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Both sects do acknowledge that the 12th Anga (Drishtivaada) has been lost, but this is not 'the only point of canonical agreement.' The two sects share extensive common ground — the 24 Tirthankara framework, the five Mahavratas, core cosmological concepts, and ethical principles. The qualifier 'only' converts a partial truth into a false absolute.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The Digambara position goes beyond merely rejecting the Valabhi council's authority. Digambaras hold that Mahavira's original teachings (the Agamas as originally delivered) have been entirely lost and are irrecoverable — a more philosophically radical stance than simply disputing the Valabhi council's legitimacy.

Value Addition:
• The 11 surviving Angas accepted by Shvetambaras include texts on cosmology, ethics, and biographical narratives of Mahavira.
• Digambara philosophical texts like Tattvartha Sutra (attributed to Umasvati) are accepted by both sects — a rare cross-sectarian canonical text.
• Drishtivaada is believed to have contained advanced philosophical content including the Purvas — even older canonical material.

solution.concept_anchor: Monastic implements — Shvetambara vs. Digambara monks
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because muhapatti is indeed a Shvetambara monastic implement, but assigning it specifically to Digambara monks reverses its correct attribution, testing whether students have fixed the sect-implement mapping precisely.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option a: The pichchhi (peacock-feather broom) is used by Digambara monks, not Shvetambara monks — this is a Digambara-Shvetambara swap.
Eliminate option b: Muhapatti (mouth-shield) is used by Shvetambara monks (and Sthanakvasi specifically) — not Digambara. This reverses the correct attribution.
Eliminate option c: The rajoharan (broom) is used by Shvetambara monks alongside the muhapatti — assigning it to Digambara monks is incorrect.
Confirm option d: Digambara monks use only a pichchhi (peacock-feather broom) to brush away insects before sitting or lying down — this is the correctly matched pair.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The pichchhi and muhapatti are both Jain monastic implements, but they belong to different sects — pichchhi to Digambara, muhapatti to Shvetambara. Options a, b, and c all involve cross-sect attribute swapping. A student who knows one implement but not its sect attribution will be vulnerable to all three wrong options. Option b is specifically designed to catch students who know muhapatti is a Jain item without having fixed it to the Shvetambara tradition.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain monastic implements are sectarian markers and are directly testable in culture and art-history questions.

• Option (a): Incorrect. The pichchhi (peacock-feather broom) is used by Digambara monks — not Shvetambara. This swaps the sect attribution.
• Option (b): Incorrect. The muhapatti (mouth-shield or face-cloth) is used by Shvetambara monks, particularly Sthanakvasi monks, to prevent harm to airborne micro-organisms. Assigning it to Digambara reverses the correct attribution.
• Option (c): Incorrect. The rajoharan (broom for sweeping the path before walking, to avoid harming insects) is a Shvetambara monastic implement, not Digambara.
• Option (d): Correct. Digambara monks carry only a pichchhi — a broom made of peacock feathers shed naturally (collected without killing) — used to gently brush away insects before sitting or lying down, expressing ahimsa in monastic practice. Digambara monks carry no other implement, consistent with their renunciation of all possessions.

Value Addition:
• Digambara monks also carry a kamandalu (water gourd) in some sub-traditions — though strict Digambara practice minimises even this.
• Shvetambara Terapanthi monks carry both muhapatti and rajoharan under strict central Acharya regulation.
• The peacock feathers used for the pichchhi must be naturally shed — collecting them is itself a form of ahimsa practice.

solution.concept_anchor: Jain karma as pudgala — physical substance
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option c is deceptive because 'karmic residue (vasana)' is a genuine concept from Hindu philosophy that describes something analogous to karma's accumulation, and a student confusing Jain and Hindu karma frameworks may select it as the correct technical term.
elimination_logic: The blank requires the Jain philosophical term for the category of matter to which karma belongs — the sentence is about karma as a physical substance.
Pudgala is the Jain term for matter or physical substance — karma in Jain philosophy is a specific type of pudgala that adheres to the soul.
Eliminate option a: 'Dharma' in Jain philosophy refers to a medium of motion, not to karma or matter.
Eliminate options c and d: 'Karmic residue (vasana)' is Hindu; 'sankhara' is Buddhist — neither belongs to the Jain philosophical framework for karma.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option c introduces a term (vasana) from Hindu philosophy that describes a similar concept — the latent impressions left by past actions — making it a plausible cross-tradition confusion. A student who has not precisely fixed the Jain term 'pudgala' as the category for karma-as-matter may select vasana because it sounds conceptually adjacent. This conflation between Jain, Hindu, and Buddhist karma terminologies is a recognised exam trap.
solution.final_explanation:
Jain karma theory is philosophically distinctive, and the term 'pudgala' is its key technical anchor.

• Option (a): Incorrect. In Jain metaphysics, 'Dharma' (dharmastikaya) refers to one of the five eternal substances — specifically the medium of motion. It does not describe the substance to which karma belongs.
• Option (b): Correct. 'Pudgala' is the Jain philosophical category for physical matter. Karma in Jain philosophy is described as a fine, subtle form of pudgala — a material substance that adheres to the jiva (soul) based on thought, word, and deed. This makes Jain karma uniquely materialist compared to Hindu or Buddhist conceptions.
• Option (c): Incorrect. 'Vasana' is a concept from Hindu/Vedantic philosophy referring to latent impressions left by past experiences and actions — not a Jain term.
• Option (d): Incorrect. 'Sankhara' (or samskara) is a Buddhist term from the Pali canon referring to mental formations or volitional activities — not a Jain philosophical term for karma.

Value Addition:
• The six dravyas (eternal substances) in Jain philosophy: jiva (soul), pudgala (matter), dharma (medium of motion), adharma (medium of rest), akasha (space), kala (time).
• Karma as pudgala means it can literally be 'shed' (nirjara) through austerity — a physical metaphor consistent with extreme asceticism.

solution.concept_anchor: Malli — 19th Tirthankara gender dispute; embryo transfer

statement_analysis.statement: The Shvetambara tradition identifies Malli, the 19th Tirthankara, as female — making the claim that a woman can attain Tirthankara status a direct Shvetambara theological argument for female liberation.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately states the Shvetambara position: Malli is identified as female, and this identification directly supports the Shvetambara claim that women can attain moksha and Tirthankara status.

statement_analysis.statement: The Digambara tradition accepts the Shvetambara account of Malli's gender but argues that this represents an exceptional case rather than proof that all women can achieve liberation.
statement_analysis.reason: Digambaras do not accept Malli as female — they insist Malli was male. The Digambara position is not that Malli is an exceptional female Tirthankara; it is a direct denial of Malli's female identity.

statement_analysis.statement: The story of Mahavira's embryo being transferred from the womb of a Brahmin woman (Devananda) to the womb of a Kshatriya woman (Trishala) is a narrative accepted by both major Jain sects as a historical fact.
statement_analysis.reason: The embryo-transfer story is exclusively a Shvetambara narrative. Digambaras completely reject it — holding that such a story contradicts Mahavira's elevated spiritual status and is a later interpolation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option a is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is clearly correct, and students who identify only Statement 3 as incorrect might miss that Statement 2 is also wrong — the Digambara position is not an 'exceptional case' argument but a flat denial of Malli's female identity.
elimination_logic: Check Statement 1: Shvetambara identifying Malli as female to support female liberation theology — accurately stated. Statement 1 is correct, not a candidate.
Check Statement 2: Digambaras do not accept Malli as female — they deny Malli's female identity entirely. The 'exceptional case' framing is fabricated. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Check Statement 3: The embryo-transfer story is Shvetambara-only — Digambaras reject it entirely. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect — the answer is option c (2 and 3 only).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a sophisticated distractor: it correctly notes there is a Digambara counter-argument about Malli but misrepresents what that counter-argument is. The Digambara position is not 'yes, Malli was female but it's an exception' — it is a categorical denial that Malli was female. Students who know there is a Digambara counter-position but are unclear on its precise nature will accept Statement 2's softened version as plausible.
solution.final_explanation:
The Malli gender dispute and the embryo-transfer narrative are two of the most precisely testable sectarian disagreements in Jain history.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Shvetambaras identify Malli (19th Tirthankara) as female and use this as a direct theological argument: if a woman can attain Tirthankara status, women are clearly capable of the highest liberation. This is the Shvetambara position on female moksha.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Digambaras do not accept Malli as female under any framing. They insist Malli was male and that the Shvetambara identification is a textual corruption or fabrication. There is no 'exceptional case' concession — it is a flat denial.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The story of the embryo transfer from Devananda (Brahmin woman) to Trishala (Kshatriya woman) appears in Shvetambara texts such as the Acharanga Sutra. Digambaras reject this narrative entirely, holding it contradicts Mahavira's pure spiritual lineage.

Value Addition:
• Parshvanatha (23rd Tirthankara) is accepted by both sects as a historical figure — his four-vow system (chaturyama) preceded Mahavira's five-vow system.
• The gender of Malli is sometimes framed as the most direct canonical disagreement — different texts of the two sects give different names and genders.
• Both sects agree that Mahavira was born a Kshatriya — the embryo-transfer story concerns the location of gestation, not Mahavira's ultimate caste identity.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option b is a strong distractor because Kumbh Mela also occurs on a 12-year cycle at specific sacred sites, and students may confuse the periodicity as the defining feature and associate the described ritual with Hindu practice rather than the Jain Digambara tradition.

Eliminate option b: The Kumbh Mela occurs on a 12-year cycle but involves river immersion, not statue-anointing — it is a Hindu practice at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, or Nashik, not Karnataka.

Eliminate options c and d: Pushkaram is a river festival; the Brahmotsavam is a Vaishnava festival — neither matches the description. The answer is option a: Mahamastakabhisheka, a Digambara Jain ritual.

solution.final_explanation:
This scenario describes Mahamastakabhisheka — the head-anointing ceremony performed at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka, every 12 years.

The Gomateshwara (Bahubali) statue at Shravanabelagola is a 57-foot monolithic sculpture of Bahubali, the son of the first Tirthankara Rishabhanatha. It is the defining Digambara monument. During Mahamastakabhisheka, the statue is anointed from head to toe with milk, sugarcane juice, saffron, and other sacred substances — the largest such Jain ceremony in India.

• Option (a): Correct. Mahamastakabhisheka is the Digambara Jain head-anointing ritual held every 12 years at Shravanabelagola, Karnataka. All details match — location, cycle, sect, nature of the ritual.
• Option (b): Incorrect. Kumbh Mela does occur every 12 years (Purna Kumbh) but is a Hindu river-bathing festival held at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, or Nashik — not a Karnataka statue-anointing ceremony.
• Option (c): Incorrect. Pushkaram is a river festival in South India occurring on a 12-year cycle tied to Jupiter's position — it involves river bathing, not statue anointing, and is not Jain.
• Option (d): Incorrect. Brahmotsavam is a major Vaishnava festival associated with temples such as Tirupati — it is not related to Jainism or monolithic statue anointing.

Value Addition:
• Mahamastakabhisheka was last held in 2018; the next is expected in 2030.
• The Gomateshwara statue was commissioned by Chavundaraya, a minister of the Ganga king Rachamalla IV, in approximately the 10th century CE.
• The statue's nudity is an explicit Digambara iconographic marker — Bahubali is depicted as having achieved liberation and stands in kayotsarga (meditating in a standing posture) with vines growing around his legs, symbolising years of motionless meditation.
